titre_chapitre: Control of Production Costs and Paradigm Shift

questions.enonce: What was the traditional historical economic relationship regarding production costs and retail price?
options: Production Costs + Profit Margin = Retail Price[span_0](start_span)[span_0](end_span)
Retail Price - Desired Profit Margin = Production Costs[span_1](start_span)[span_1](end_span)
Retail Price + Production Costs = Profit Margin
Profit Margin - Production Costs = Retail Price
questions.explication: Historically, companies determined their retail price by adding their production costs and desired profit margin together[span_2](start_span)[span_2](end_span).

questions.enonce: What represents the modern paradigm shift in the pricing equation described in the course?
options: Production costs are fixed by the company and retail price adjusts freely.
Retail Price - Desired Profit Margin = Production Costs[span_3](start_span)[span_3](end_span)
Profit margin becomes zero, making production costs equal to retail price.
The market sets production costs directly as an input.
questions.explication: The equation was reversed because retail prices are increasingly constrained and set by the market, making production costs a target to achieve[span_4](start_span)[span_4](end_span).

questions.enonce: Why is a good demand forecast essential for controlling production costs?
options: It eliminates the need for workforce training.

It prevents overproduction (which creates costly excess stock) and underproduction (which causes lost sales), both of which negatively impact unit production costs[span_5](start_span)[span_5](end_span).
It allows the company to ignore market competition completely.
It guarantees that equipment will always operate at exactly 30% capacity.
questions.explication: Poor demand forecasting leads either to costly excess stock from overproducing or lost sales from underproducing, both of which worsen unit production costs[span_6](start_span)[span_6](end_span).

questions.enonce: How does equipment utilization affect production costs, as discussed in the introduction?
options: Using expensive equipment at a low rate (e.g., 30% capacity) makes for a bad investment that negatively affects costs[span_7](start_span)[span_7](end_span).
Low equipment utilization improves product quality and lowers costs.
Equipment utilization has no impact on production costs as long as the retail price is fixed.
Higher utilization always guarantees zero inventory.
questions.explication: Investing in super equipment and only using it at a fraction of its capacity (like 30%) represents a poor investment that harms production costs[span_8](start_span)[span_8](end_span).

questions.enonce: Why is flexibility required in a company's production capacities over the year?
options: Because market demand and required workloads vary across different seasons[span_9](start_span)[span_9](end_span).
Because equipment never experiences maintenance or breakdowns.
To ensure that all employees work fixed, unchanging hours every single day.
Because retail prices change every hour.
questions.explication: Flexibility is needed because different seasons may require higher or lower workloads to match varying market demand[span_10](start_span)[span_10](end_span).
